size.note: Sexed mass follows the description section of the Wikipedia Cape bushbuck article (males 60–80 kg, females 25–60 kg). The same article's opening sentence gives an unsexed range of 45–80 kg, which overlaps those figures. Shoulder height is given only as 'around 90 cm', so shoulderHeightCm is omitted. Male horns are described as over half a metre long, with a single twist. Head-and-body and tail lengths were not found as published ranges.

summary: A medium-sized, usually solitary spiral-horned antelope of thickets and forest edge. The coat is light brown, with white spots and up to seven white stripes, a white muzzle, and white marks on the ears, chin, neck, legs and tail. Only males have horns. Kruger holds a resident population, but no recent park count was found.
description: Cape or southern bushbuck, the form in Kruger, have a light brown coat with up to seven white stripes and geometrically shaped white splotches on the sides, and further white marks on the most mobile parts: the ears, chin, tail, legs and neck. The muzzle is white. Only males have horns; these are more than half a metre long and have a single twist. Young males sprout particularly twisted horns from about ten months, and the first loop of the spiral forms at maturity. Females are smaller and hornless. The species was listed on the 2011 SANParks checklist as Tragelaphus scriptus; the Kruger taxon is stored here as Tragelaphus sylvaticus.
habits: Bushbuck are generally solitary, but they are not aggressively antisocial, and individuals sometimes forage close together. Each animal lives in a home area, often around five hectares on savanna and larger in forest, which usually overlaps those of others. They browse rather than graze, and they are active through the day, becoming more nocturnal near people. In Kruger they are often seen in riverine thickets and around rest camps.

diet.summary: A browser of trees, shrubs and forbs; they rarely if ever eat grasses. In south-eastern Africa they frequently take acacias and other legumes, mallows such as Grewia and Hibiscus, bushwillows, and buckthorns.
items: Grewia, Hibiscus, Combretum and related browse

young: A detailed account of gestation length and calving months for this species was not found in the sources used here. Young animals resemble the female in coat and, in males, later grow short horns. A suckling calf in the Kruger photographs already shows the white spots of the adult coat. Exact calving months for Kruger were not found.
habitat: A wide range of cover, including woodland, bushveld, thickets and forest edge. In Kruger it is typically seen in riverine thickets and around camps.

similar.note: The bushbuck is a smaller, usually solitary antelope. The male's horns have a single twist, and both sexes show white spots and up to seven stripes on a light brown coat.
The bushbuck is much smaller, with shorter, single-twist horns in the male only, and a spotted, lightly striped coat.

population.notes: No recent Kruger population figure was found. The EWT assessment cites a 2009 count of about 500 animals in Kruger (Ferreira et al. 2013), kept here as a previous estimate. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. Regional Red List status is Least Concern, with a regional trend described as stable.

previousEstimates.notes: Kruger only, given as 'c. 500 individuals (2009 count)' on the EWT Southern Bushbuck page, citing Ferreira et al. 2013.
